evidence.paraphrase: Kaśyapa teaches Vāmana the four Vedas with their limbs. Vāmana asks how to restore the gods’ offices and remove the earth’s burden. His father teaches a six-syllable mantra pleasing to Vighneśa, and urges effort because a pleased Lord fulfills all desires. Vāmana bows, obtains permission and leaves the āśrama. At a wooded, lake-adorned site in Vidarbha he sits in lotus posture, controls his senses, fasts and recites for ONE YEAR. Gajānana appears with Siddhi and Buddhi, riding a peacock, with ten arms, trunk, jewel garland, ornaments and a snake at the navel. His light surpasses other lights; Vāmana praises the giver of accomplishments and remover of obstacles.

evidence.paraphrase: Vāmana’s hymn praises the unmanifest cause, known through Vedānta, beyond māyā, assuming bodies for devotees and giving enjoyment and liberation. Pleased by the hymn and tapas, Gajānana invites a boon. Vāmana says the vision is enough, but to honor the deity’s word asks never to be defeated and never to fear obstacles in any task. He mentions Bali seeking Indra’s office through ritual, and asks success for the purpose of the one who sought refuge. The pronoun in31.19 does not repeat that person’s name. Gajānana grants everything through remembrance of himself: great and small tasks will succeed.

evidence.paraphrase: After the Lord departs, Vāmana commissions and installs a Kashmir-stone image with four arms, three eyes, trunk and a benignant elephant hand. It grants fearlessness and all desires through remembrance, sight, meditation and worship. He builds a temple of gems and gold, appoints an unnamed brāhmaṇa and gives a village and wealth for worship three times daily. Returning home, he bows to Kaśyapa, reports his tapas and its fruit, and seeks permission to attend the sacrifice. With permission, wearing sacred thread, black deer skin and girdle and carrying a darbha staff, he approaches Bali’s sacrifice. The sages marvel at the short child’s extraordinary radiance.

evidence.paraphrase: Bali rises, bows and asks Vāmana’s identity, origin, parents, home and desire. Vāmana says he does not remember his parents, asks to be known as an orphan, claims residence in the three worlds and requests three steps of land for a leaf hut. As compassionate Bali prepares the gift, Kāvya—explicitly captioned Śukra—warns that disguised Hari will take the three worlds and advises giving nothing. Bali rejects this counsel: if Hari leaves disappointed, his merit will be lost; no better recipient exists and such a gift has infinite fruit. He grants the land and asks for the formal intention to be made.

evidence.paraphrase: Kīrti worships and sings the hymn daily. Her friends cannot find dūrvā in Śukra month and bring śamī leaves instead. Hymn reading gives influence over king and others, progeny, wealth, Vedic learning and stronger intelligence; reading three times daily gives desired ends, firm devotion and final liberation. Viṣṇu assumes the explicitly named Mohinī form and promises to be the demon’s woman if he obeys. He agrees and imitates every dance gesture. She puts her hand on her own head; he copies and becomes ashes. Mukunda remains in the city, whose worshippers gain immediate accomplishment, while Mohinī gives devotional wishes. Durāsada later rules the three worlds from there.

evidence.paraphrase: Answering Durāsada’s boast, his ministers say Avimukta, the incomparable tenth region where Śiva lives, remains unconquered. He goes there by flying vehicle; alarm spreads and gods disappear. Because Durāsada is his devotee, Śiva does not become angry: he acknowledges the temporary grant and withdraws with his retinue to Kedāra. Sages flee except the field-renunciant Jaigīṣavya. Durāsada breaks images and temples, beats and expels those remembering gods, and suppresses offerings, Vedic and śāstra study, Purāṇa recitation, worship, vows and circumambulation. With ritual conduct and dharma lost, the gods become hungry.

narrative_events.details: Kaśyapa teaches the Vedas and initiates Vāmana with six syllables for restoring divine offices. After permission, the child practices one YEAR of fasting japa in Vidarbha. A ten-armed, peacock-mounted Gajānana appears with Siddhi and Buddhi.

Vāmana hymns the Lord. Reluctant to ask after receiving the vision, he nevertheless requests freedom from defeat and obstacles and success for the refuge-seeker’s purpose. The Lord grants all great and small tasks through remembrance.

Vāmana installs the four-armed, three-eyed Kashmir-stone image, builds its temple and endows a priest for worship three times daily. He reports to Kaśyapa and obtains permission to visit Bali’s sacrifice, where sages marvel at him.

Bali asks the visitor’s identity and desire. Vāmana performs an orphan claim and asks three steps of land for a hut. Śukra/Kāvya warns that he is Hari seeking the three worlds, but Bali chooses the infinite merit of the gift and formally grants it.

The printed Śakra water-stopper and śalākā episode remain under review. Water is given; Vāmana remembers Gaṇeśa and grows. The literal sequence gives heaven to his head, rodasī to one foot, nether regions to another and another placement on Bali’s head.
Ordered to Dharaṇītala, Bali asks how he could go without the Lord. Vāmana promises presence and later Indra’s office after the current holder’s tenure, while honoring Indra’s earlier refuge first.

Gods praise and celebrate, Vāmana vanishes and they return to their former places. His image becomes famous as a desire-giver. The Adosha and orientation clause is retained before the promised śamī explanation.
Brahmā reports the Lord’s śamī teaching to Priyavrata. Vyāsa asks the king’s identity; a nested Śiva–Pārvatī conversation opens his history.

Priyavrata’s wives and ministers are introduced. Prabhā wins his preference while Kīrti is rejected. Prabhā’s son receives rites, initiation and a princess’s marriage; the first wife is reduced to service and kicked down.
Kīrti despairs and considers Hari’s aid to Draupadī. Devala teaches Gajānana worship. She worships the Mandāra image with sixteen services and a hymn framed by five-deity non-difference.

Unable to obtain dūrvā, her friends bring śamī. At year’s end a dream gives unsolicited marital and son grants, predicts fourth-year poison death and Gṛtsamada’s revival, and promises hymn-reading fruits.

After completing her vow, Kīrti waits. Prabhā’s illness changes the king’s preference; Kīrti bears the promised son. Jealous Prabhā gives poison, physicians fail, she is expelled and the child dies as his mother takes him into the forest.

Gṛtsamada hears the grieving mother’s refuge request. He orders transfer of the śamī-worship merit into the child’s hand, and the boy rises. Kīrti reports the messengers’ battle and asks how the sage knew and why the leaf has this power.
Gṛtsamada describes the leaf’s superior devotional merit and introduces Nārada’s conversation with Indra before continuing the frame.
Nārada tells Indra about Aurava, Sumedhā and Śamikā. Their daughter marries Dhaumya’s son Mandāra, Śaunaka’s disciple, and later joins her husband after her father’s loving protection request.
The couple laugh at Bhṛśuṇḍī’s tapas-grown trunk. He curses them to shunned trees, adding release when the trunked Lord is pleased. They become Mandāra and thorny śamī.
After a month, the father and guru search and learn the curse through meditation. Seeking relief for daughter and disciple, they perform twelve YEARS of fasting, one-toe, six-syllable tapas.
A ten-armed, lion-mounted, noose-bearing Lord appears. The sages hymn him and receive an invitation to request boons, together with specific hymn-reading promises.

They request removal of treehood. Gaṇeśa refuses to annul his devotee’s word and gives permanent root-presence instead, with favored-offering substitutions and devotional benefits. He actually dwells at both roots.

Aurava’s tapas, heavenly departure and fire transformation are retained without an invented sequence. Śaunaka creates a Mandāra-root image, receives unspecified grants and returns to worship. Gṛtsamada explains why śamī became dear.
At Mahābala, the hurried sacrifice neglects Gaṇeśa and Sāvitrī and seats Gāyatrī. Sāvitrī’s curse becomes river forms at the petitioners’ request, including Śiva/Veṇyā and Kṛṣṇa/Kṛṣṇā.
Brahmā and the goddesses acknowledge the neglected worship and plan devotion. The women go to the Rāma-established Vakratunda image in Karnāṭaka; his victory is recalled briefly.
Varied austerities initially fail. Following a sky instruction, all offer śamī leaves and receive the four-armed, TWO-TUSK, mouse-mounted vision with Siddhi and Buddhi.
The goddess hymn requests original forms and constant remembrance. Gaṇeśa preserves Sāvitrī’s curse through river portions while restoring gods’ forms and offices. They apologize and worship.
Gods install the stone Heramba temple at Supattana; Indra takes the earlier Mandāra image. Divine offices and household joys return. Brahmā performs twelve YEARS of tapas and repeats the sacrifice.

Gṛtsamada applies the plant account to the child’s revival and asks to leave. Kīrti bows and dismisses him; devotional hearing and morning remembrance fruits close the account, before another question in38.

Because the child cannot recite six syllables, Kīrti asks for a simpler royal-success mantra. Gṛtsamada proposes the four-syllable Dhundhirāja name. Her origin questions introduce Skanda’s account to Agastya.
The account explains creation classes, merit and holy fields, Kāśī, Maṇikarṇikā and Bhāgīrathī, name and death efficacy and five-god unity. The birth-class numerical relation remains unresolved.
Bhasmāsura’s son receives Śukra’s five-syllable instruction and practices1000DIVINE YEARS. A ten-armed, five-faced Śiva appears, receives the hymn and invites rare wishes.

Durāsada requests broad protection, terror, kingdom and devotion. Śiva explicitly grants protection from gods with one Śakti exception, a radiance-born conqueror who keeps him alive under a foot, and renewed conquest if that foot is removed.
Armed with two ministers and a fourfold host, the demon takes earthly kingdoms and divine offices. Gods retreat, and he rules from Bhāsmaka/Mukundapura.

The flashback gives Bhasmāsura’s head-touch boon and pursuit of its donor. Mohinī’s dance imitation causes his own fatal head touch, after which the city is associated with Mukunda and her devotional favors.
Ministers direct Durāsada to still-unconquered Avimukta. Śiva withdraws to Kedāra, Jaigīṣavya remains, temples and worship are suppressed, and lost ritual nourishment leaves gods hungry.
Brahmā identifies the Śiva grant and the Śakti-radiance child as its exception. Gods and sages are directed first to Pārvatī, then to the cosmic Gaṇeśa.
Bhavānī accepts praise and directs a Gaṇeśa hymn. A sky voice assures the counter; petitioners seek explanation from Pārvatī while Śiva meditates.

Pārvatī’s mouth, nose and eyes emit radiance that becomes a ten-armed, ten-weapon Vināyaka. She worships, names him Vakratunda, gives her lion and requests the demon’s defeat and restored divine offices.
Vakratunda accepts his mother’s request and rides to Kāśī; he indicts Durāsada’s abuses and offers surrender before raising the axe.

Axe heart-strike leaves even a hair unmoved. Goad checks sword and axe breaks it into100pieces. Matching-growth wrestling continues many days; forehead punch leaves demon unconscious2muhūrtas, revived recognizing weakness.
Fire→rain counter; wind disperses rain→mountains counter; Raudra/Brahmā weapons collide and burn people/army; dual cessation agency unresolved. Demon leaves ministers to fight while he eats.
Lord’s56 varied mounted/armed forms dismantle host; surrender, flight and face-to-face death/heaven outcomes. Demon returns to dead host, recalls Śakti exception and flees.

Respecting fleeing-foe rule and Śiva nondeath boon, Virāṭa captures and holds demon by foot. Grants immovable gateway role, wicked suppression and continuing nearness; demon asks permanent foot, Lord assents.
Earth auspicious, gods/sages return offices, worshippers’ wishes fulfilled;56forms inKāśī and Eka-pāda inTuṇḍana after Virāṭa contraction; story phalas.

Praise restores ritual ways/office, Dhundhi/rāja name derived from search/function assignment; four-aim/progeny promise. Plant/food/gem worship,56Vināyakas/seven enclosures/five-faced doorway figure, cosmic duties resume. Divodāsa branch announced next.
